source.authors: Kourakis MJ, Borba C, Zhang A, Newman-Smith E, Salas P, Manjunath B, Smith WC
source.title: Parallel visual circuitry in a basal chordate

quote: The first circuit is characterized by glutamatergic photoreceptors and responds to the direction of light.
note: Licence: Crossref lists CC BY 4.0 for the version of record. The Methods name two species: Ciona intestinalis type B (Marine Biological Laboratory, Woods Hole), used for the in situ maps (staged to match the connectome larva; the connectome paper's title names Ciona intestinalis) and for microinjection, and Ciona robusta (formerly C. intestinalis type A; Santa Barbara harbour and M-REP), used for the electroporated reporter constructs and the pVGAT>kaede stable line behind the coexpression figures. The Methods do not say which species the behavioural larvae were. The circuits were predicted from the larval connectome and mapped by neurotransmitter expression, then tested with behaviour: negative phototaxis (505 nm LED at one side of a 10 cm dish) in control and perampanel-treated larvae, and the dimming response. The Discussion says the proposed disinhibitory circuit of the second pathway still needs validation: 'Validation of this hypothetical disinhibitory circuit will require analysis of individual neurons in behaving larvae.' The authors could not image the photoreceptors with GCaMP because its spectra overlap the larvae's behavioural spectrum and it is poor at showing inhibition, so no photoreceptor recordings were made. frm mutants lacking photoreceptors showed no response to light (the authors' unpublished observation). The Introduction cites earlier work (Salas et al. 2018) for the dimming response being mediated by PR-II 'likely with a contribution from the PR-Is'. Abstract read on the open publisher page and the PMC copy. The Introduction says the PR-I outer segments project into the cup-shaped pigment cell, making the group sensitive to the direction of incident light and mediating negative phototaxis (cited to Horie et al. 2008a and Salas et al. 2018). Filed under C. intestinalis because the glutamatergic and GABAergic identities rest on the type B in situ maps and the connectome.

source.title: Functional characterization of optic photoreception in Lymnaea stagnalis

quote: The two pigmented eyes (red chevrons) thought to form the basis of binocular vision in L. stagnalis sit adjacent to tentacles (yellow chevrons) extending from the head (Fig 1A).
note: Licence: Crossref lists CC BY 4.0 for the version of record. The binocular-vision role is the authors' hedged suggestion ('thought to form the basis'); no binocular overlap was measured. The paper describes a cup-shaped eye with a lens in a vitreous body and a four-layer retina (epithelial, pigment, nucleated somatic, neuronal). The text gives pigment granule sizes of 250 to 500 um, which looks like a unit error, and was not used. Full text read on the publisher page (journals.plos.org); the PMC copy was blocked.

value: positive locomotory response to intense focal light; diverse photo-locomotory responses
eye: not shown to be the eyes: eyes were not ablated, and the Discussion raises non-ocular photoreceptors driving locomotion independent of ocular photoreception
method: neurobehavioural arena: snails tracked with DeepLabCut through room-light acclimation, a dark phase and a focal-light phase
conditions: n = 29 snails, lab-raised, 2 to 3 months old, 20 to 30 mm; 15 min per testing phase; 20 to 22 C; light intensity, wavelength and arena size not reported in the main text; 23 snails were classed strong responders and 6 weak responders (79.3% and 20.7%), though the Results print the strong group as 23/26 while the cohort is 29

source.authors: Harracksingh AN, Bandura J, Morizumi T, Monnier PP, Henderson JT, Feng ZP
source.title: Functional characterization of optic photoreception in Lymnaea stagnalis

quote: We demonstrated that L. stagnalis exhibits a positive locomotory response to intense focal light and has diverse photo-locomotory responses.
note: Licence: Crossref lists CC BY 4.0 for the version of record. Strong responders travelled about 86.85 +/- 4.235 cm in the focal-light phase against 44.58 +/- 5.081 cm in the dark (p < 0.0001); weak responders about 34.63 +/- 5.562 cm against 12.95 +/- 3.318 cm (p = 0.0068). The paper does not test wavelength or intensity dependence, and the Discussion does not say whether the eyes are necessary for the response; it mentions non-ocular photoreceptors that drive locomotion independent of ocular photoreception and suggests the statocyst's role in phototaxis for future work. Full text read on the publisher page; the PMC copy was blocked. Responses were scored as distance travelled per phase (two-way ANOVA with Tukey tests, +/- SEM), not as movement toward the source.
